question:
(a) Determine all real $x$ satisfying $\sin^{-1}x=\cos^{-1}\sqrt{1-x^2}$ by carefully applying the domain and sign restrictions.

(b) Verify the obtained solution set using the principal-value ranges of both inverse functions.
explanation:
(a)
The expression $\sin^{-1}x$ requires $-1\leq x\leq1$. For this interval, $\sqrt{1-x^2}$ lies in $[0,1]$, so the inverse-cosine expression is also defined.
Let
$$\theta=\sin^{-1}x$$
Then
$$\sin\theta=x,\qquad -\frac{\pi}{2}\leq\theta\leq\frac{\pi}{2}$$
Also,
$$\cos\theta=\sqrt{1-x^2}$$
because $\cos\theta$ is non-negative throughout this interval. Therefore,
$$\cos^{-1}\sqrt{1-x^2}=\cos^{-1}(\cos\theta)$$
Since $\cos^{-1}$ returns a value in $[0,\pi]$,
$$\cos^{-1}(\cos\theta)=|\theta|$$
The given equation becomes
$$\theta=|\theta|$$
This holds exactly when $\theta\geq0$. Since $\sin^{-1}x$ has the same sign as $x$, the required condition is $x\geq0$. Combining this with $-1\leq x\leq1$ gives
$$0\leq x\leq1$$

(b)
For every $x\in[0,1]$, let $\theta=\sin^{-1}x$. Then $\theta\in\left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ and
$$\sqrt{1-x^2}=\cos\theta$$
Thus,
$$\cos^{-1}\sqrt{1-x^2}=\cos^{-1}(\cos\theta)=\theta=\sin^{-1}x$$
For $x<0$, $\sin^{-1}x<0$, whereas $\cos^{-1}\sqrt{1-x^2}\geq0$, so equality is impossible. Hence, the solution set is $[0,1]$.

options.A:
(a) $x\in[-1,1]$

(b) Both inverse expressions are equal throughout their complete common domain
options.B:
(a) $x\in[-1,0]$

(b) Equality holds because both inverse expressions have non-positive principal values
options.C:
(a) $x=0$ only

(b) Equality fails for every non-zero value because the principal-value ranges are different
options.D:
(a) $x\in[0,1]$

(b) For these values, both sides lie in $\left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ and are equal; for $x<0$, the left side is negative while the right side is non-negative
